title: Value types and reference types
sub: Why the same line behaves differently
cards/0/body:
Every type in C# is one of two kinds.

Value types: int, double, bool, any struct. The variable holds the value itself.

Reference types: any class, string, arrays. The variable holds only the object's address, a reference. The object itself lives elsewhere, on the heap.

A value type is like a note with a number on it: you hand over a copy and keep your own. A reference type is like a house address: give it to a friend, and you both walk into the same house.
cards/1/task: Step through the program twice: once with Point as a struct and once as a class. Watch the stack and the heap.
cards/1/variants/struct/steps/0/note: p1 is a struct: both fields live right in the variable, on the stack.
cards/1/variants/struct/steps/1/note: p2 = p1 copies the whole struct. Now there are two independent points.
cards/1/variants/struct/steps/2/note: We change p2. p1 is not affected.
cards/1/variants/struct/steps/3/note: Prints 1: p1 has its own copy.
cards/1/variants/class/steps/0/note: A Point object is created on the heap. p1 holds only a reference to it.
cards/1/variants/class/steps/1/note: p2 = p1 copies the reference. Both variables lead to the same object.
cards/1/variants/class/steps/2/note: We change the object through p2. It's the same object p1 points to.
cards/1/variants/class/steps/3/note: Prints 100: p1 and p2 are the same object.
cards/2/q: Point is a struct. What does the code print?
cards/2/explain: Assigning a struct copies all of it. p2 is a separate copy, and changes to it don't show up in p1.
cards/3/q: And if Point is a class?
cards/3/explain: For a class, only the reference is copied. p1 and p2 lead to one object, so a change made through p2 is visible through p1.
cards/4/q: Which of these are value types? Select all that apply.
cards/4/explain: DateTime is a struct. string and arrays are reference types, even if they hold nothing but numbers.
cards/5/title: How to tell which is which
cards/5/body:
struct and enum are value types. class, interface, delegates, arrays and string are reference types.

Can't remember? Hover over the type in your IDE: it will say struct or class.
cards/5/deep: A record struct is a value type; a plain record (a record class) is a reference type. int? is Nullable<int>, also a struct: the value plus a HasValue flag.
cards/6/q: Point is a class with no Equals override. What does a.Equals(b) return?
cards/6/explain: These are two different objects on the heap. A class's default Equals compares references. For a struct it would compare fields and return True.
cards/6/wrong/1: A struct would give True: its default Equals compares fields.
cards/7/q: When does a struct make sense?
cards/7/options/0: A small value that behaves like a number: a coordinate, a color, a date
cards/7/options/1: A big object with a dozen fields that gets passed around a lot
cards/7/options/2: An object that is modified from many places in the program
cards/7/explain: A struct is copied on every assignment and every call. That's expensive for big data, and changes to a copy don't reach the original.
cards/7/deep: Microsoft's guideline: a struct should be under 16 bytes, immutable, and logically represent a single value.
cards/8/q: Point is a class. After which line does a.X become 50?
cards/8/explain: b is a reference to the same object as a. c is a completely different object, even though it has the same values.
